newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street scorns Clinton budget's rosy outlook.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street scorns Clinton budget's rosy outlook.

text.p: Wall Street professionals lambasted the rosy economic assumptions behind President Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget blueprint, saying such ideal deficit-reducing conditions were almost certainly unattainable.

"There's a lot of, I don't even want to call it smoke and mirrors, it's just plain garbage that is embedded in how they got to a surplus budget in 2002," said Michael Strauss, senior vice president and chief economist at Sanwa Securities in New York.
Clinton formally presented his budget proposal, which met his oft-stated goal of balancing the books by the year 2002, to Congress on Thursday.

Economists said the most questionable economic forecast behind the budget was a more than full-point drop in short-term Treasury yields by 2002. Most also took issue with the proposed unrelenting real economic growth at 2.3 percent and steady consumer price inflation at 2.7 percent from 1999 to 2002.

"You are not going to have short-term rates at 4.0 percent when inflation is at 3.0 percent. Those things just don't hang together," said Robert DiClemente, director of economic and market analysis at Salomon Brothers Inc.

"You can't have sustainable real interest rates at 1.0 percent. That doesn't fly," DiClemente added. Other economists said the last time real interest rates were less than one percent, inflation was in double digits.
Mickey Levy, chief financial economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc, was more forgiving than most of his peers.

He found the administration's assumptions on real economic growth and inflation reasonable. However, he too found the projected decline in real interest rates at odds with the assumed healthy economic growth.

"What economic common sense tells you is with healthy real economic growth, you should not have declining real interest rates. Real interest rates tend to mirror real economic performance," Levy said.
"I find that inconsistency despite what they would say about the positive financial market response to the lower deficit," he added.
Also, the proposal apparently assumes no increase in short-term interest rates by the Federal Reserve this year, despite expectations to the contrary by many private experts.

Bond traders noticed that the Treasury Department, in the recent launch of its new inflation-adjusted government securities, must have expected higher future inflation rates than shown in the budget forecast, or it would not have sold the bonds at the price offered.

"If the government truly believed (Clinton's inflation forecast) the dumbest thing in the world they did was issue these inflation indexed bonds at 3.447 percent," said a bond trader at a large investment bank.
"The market certainly isn't believing that forecast or they wouldn't be trading at 3.32 percent today," he added.
Stock market reaction to the budget was muted, with attention focused on Friday's release of January U.S. nonfarm payrolls data, said George Pirrone, senior equities trader at Dreyfus Corp.

Kevin Sluder, intermediate coupon trader and senior government bond trader at First Chicago Capital Markets, said the bond market had anticipated such a budget proposal and that "no one attaches a whole lot to it."

"The fact of the matter is we've been hearing the balanced budget speech forever. The market's attitude is: 'Show me.' We've heard this song so many times before, it's just not worth going through the drill again," added Joseph Benning, a long governments trader at Daiwa Securities America Inc.

Economists were also quick to note that Clinton's goal of achieving a balanced budget by 2002 ignores the mounting unfunded liability of Social Security, which could balloon the defict beginning around 2005 as baby-boomers begin to retire.

"A balanced budget by 2002 is nonsense -- trivial to the continued growing liability of unfunded Social Security. It reflects the short-term and political nature of budget making in Washington," Levy of NationsBanc said.

Sanwa's Strauss said the Social Security surplus added roughly $115 billion to the government coffers last year, but warned that starting in about the year 2002, it will be a significant drain on the system.
Market players said they were wary of acting prematurely as Clinton's budget blueprint now moves to Congressional committees, where it will undergo heavy scrutiny.

"We're going to want to see ink on the dotted line before beginning to trade on it. This year is going to be one of those 'Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me' situations," said Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston in New York.

"(The markets) are cautious because in last year's process there were so many emotional highs and lows and when all was said and done, nothing much was done. They'll be more cautious this time around."
